presentingComplaint: Severe headache, blurred vision and confusion over 12 hours with a very high home blood pressure reading
history: 12-hour history of progressively worsening throbbing headache, nausea, transient visual blurring and increasing drowsiness/confusion witnessed by family. Known essential hypertension for 8 years, poorly controlled; ran out of amlodipine and telmisartan 3 weeks ago and stopped taking them. No focal limb weakness, no chest pain, no seizure. Ex-smoker. No recreational stimulant use. No prior stroke or CKD.
examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6), no lateralising motor deficit and no neck stiffness. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilloedema (Grade IV / KWB retinopathy). Heart sounds normal, no added sounds; chest clear; no peripheral oedema. Pertinent negatives: no unilateral weakness or dysphasia (argues against acute stroke), no radio-femoral delay or inter-arm BP difference, no thunderclap onset.

labs.urinalysis: mild proteinuria, no active sediment / no RBC casts

imaging: CT head: no haemorrhage, no infarct, no mass; symmetrical subcortical/posterior white-matter hypodensity consistent with PRES-type vasogenic oedema. CXR: no pulmonary oedema.
finalDiagnosis: Hypertensive emergency with hypertensive encephalopathy (PRES) due to abrupt antihypertensive withdrawal
citations: AHA/ACC High Blood Pressure in Adults Guideline 2017
contraindications: Avoid abrupt/excessive BP reduction: lower MAP by no more than ~25% in the first hour to prevent watershed cerebral, coronary and renal hypoperfusion
Avoid sublingual short-acting nifedipine (uncontrolled precipitous drops)
Nitroprusside caution in renal impairment / prolonged use (cyanide-thiocyanate toxicity)
edgeCases: If focal deficit or acute ischaemic stroke is confirmed, permissive hypertension applies and aggressive lowering is harmful — a key pitfall
Consider secondary causes (phaeochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis, cocaine/amphetamine, eclampsia) when presentation is atypical or refractory
expectedMaiK: This is a hypertensive emergency (severe BP with acute encephalopathy and Grade IV retinopathy plus PRES on imaging), not merely severe asymptomatic hypertension. Manage with a titratable IV agent (e.g. labetalol or nicardipine) and controlled MAP reduction of ~25% in the first hour, having first excluded acute stroke where BP targets differ.
expectedNextQuestions: Any focal weakness, speech disturbance or seizure to suggest a primary intracranial event?
History of antihypertensive non-adherence, and any stimulant/recreational drug use or pregnancy?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage/infarct
Fundoscopy, ECG, U&E/creatinine, urinalysis and troponin for end-organ assessment

investigations: Fundoscopy and end-organ bloods (U&E, creatinine, troponin, urinalysis)
